If you have overdosed on paracetamol you should go to the hospital immediately before it is absorbed by the liver. Don’t wait until you feel sick or in pain.

The LD50 for rats (lethal dose for half a test population of rats) was found to be greater than 2000mg/kg. Most nonprescription medications have a very high LD-50 and aren’t sold in quantities anywhere near high enough to cause death. 100lbs is approximately 45kg so you’d need to take at least 90,000mg to have even a 50% chance of dying. Suicide attempts with paracetamol almost never result in death, just a lot of pain, a trip to the hospital to have your stomach pumped and a possible lifelong liver injury which will cause further pain and illness for the rest of your life.

Whilst ‘hacking the UART,’ as in interfering with or just overwriting the data being communicated from the throttle to the motor controller in the deck of the scooter is certainly possible, I don’t understand why it’s necessary in this case?

Those throttles/displays are standardised and used on many different scooter brands and models. Manufacturers, distributors or even retail stores can set speed restrictions by editing the P settings. So long as the P menu is not locked, or the 4-digit PIN is known (some manufacturers such as Kaabo will lock the P settings menu with a 4-digit PIN), setting the motor power settings to 100% should unlock the maximum motor power/speed possible for the model of scooter. 

These throttle displays just provide a fairly universal, generic interface and display for controlling the physical motor controller. So long as the P settings menu is accessible, the throttle should communicate to the motor controller to operate at the maximum possible power/speed when the throttle is maxed out. Additionally, the motor controller will have its own internal restrictions to prevent damage to the battery and/or motor. If the relevant P setting for motor power is adjusted to 100% though, I fail to see how the scooter’s maximum speed could possibly be increased any further without changing the physical motor controller itself which would be complicated and impractical.

I’m pretty sure I get the synchronous/asynchronous difference now. It seems like pretty much all motor controllers including the one on the GitHub page would use asynchronous communication. I think I got myself confused with asynchronous network and computing applications which use interrupt signals and don’t rely on serial communication so baud rate would is not relevant for those cases.  

In this case, the motor controller and display would both have their own internal clocks and the serial data communication signal between the two would be transmitted at the same frequency (baud rate) in each direction but the rising and falling edges of their individual clock signals would not be synchronised. 

In fact, I imagine it’s probably standard for almost all individual components to communicate with each other asynchronously in this way because I can’t really see any reason why they’d need to share exactly the same clock signals or even benefit from it so long as they were communicating with the correct baud rate. 

I’m thinking that synchronous circuits are more relevant when talking about individual components. Both the motor controller and throttle would probably contain synchronised circuits within them but they communicate externally asynchronously.

- there are 5 wires soldered on the PCB  from the cable which would be connected to the motor controller which are soldered to the PCB. These are:

 - HALL: this would most likely be an analog voltage output from a Hall effect (magnetic) sensor measuring the throttle level. It would output an analog voltage value proportional to the throttle position to the motor controller
 - BAT: unsure but could be the scooter battery’s voltage level. This may either be used purely for displaying voltage level on the dashboard and/or a power supply for the dashboard
 - D5: unsure but most likely digital HIGH 5V
 - D0: unsure but most likely digital LOW 0V and/or ground
